name: Shackleton Crater
why_it_matters: 21 km crater at the south pole. Rim gets near-continuous sunlight, interior is a permanent cold trap that may hold ice.

name: Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge
why_it_matters: Sunlit ridge joining Shackleton and de Gerlache craters. Top candidate for power and for reaching shadowed ice.

name: Mons Mouton
why_it_matters: Highland massif near the south pole with long sunlit periods and gentle slopes. Named Artemis III region.

name: Mons Mouton Plateau
why_it_matters: Flatter ground on the Mons Mouton massif, favoured for landing.

name: Peak Near Cabeus B
why_it_matters: Sunlit peak close to Cabeus, where LCROSS found water in a permanently shadowed crater.

name: Haworth
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Large polar crater with permanently shadowed floor, a candidate for water-ice access.

name: Malapert Massif
image_credit: James Stuby based on NASA image, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Tall massif with direct line of sight to Earth, useful for communications.

name: Nobile Rim 1
image_credit: Lunar_south_pole_summer.jpg: NASA derivative work: J6naspeg (talk), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Rim of Nobile crater on the far side of the south pole, partly sunlit.

name: Nobile Rim 2
image_credit: Lunar_south_pole_summer.jpg: NASA derivative work: J6naspeg (talk), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Second landing area on the Nobile crater rim.

name: de Gerlache Rim 2
image_credit: Moon_South_Pole.jpg: Image PIA00001 Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech derivative work: J, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Rim of de Gerlache crater, close to the Shackleton ridge.

name: Slater Plain
why_it_matters: Smooth plain near the pole, listed among the nine Artemis III regions.

name: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base)
image_credit: Neil A. Armstrong, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: First crewed landing, in basalt mare.

name: Apollo 12
image_credit: NASA, Alan L. Bean, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Precision landing near Surveyor 3 in Oceanus Procellarum.

name: Apollo 14 (Fra Mauro)
image_credit: Edgar D. Mitchell / NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Landing on the Fra Mauro formation, ejecta from the Imbrium basin.

name: Apollo 15 (Hadley-Apennine)
image_credit: NASA Johnson Space Center Restored by Bammesk, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: First lunar rover mission, beside Hadley Rille.

name: Apollo 16 (Descartes)
image_credit: Charlie Duke, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Highland landing in the Descartes region, reference for lunar highlands.

name: Apollo 17 (Taurus-Littrow)
image_credit: Harrison Schmitt / Apollo 17, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Valley between massifs with mare basalt and dark mantling deposits.

name: Luna 16
image_credit: Bembmv, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: First robotic sample return from another world.

name: Luna 20
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Sample return from highland terrain near Apollonius.

name: Luna 24
image_credit: LRO, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Core sample from Mare Crisium.

name: Chang'e 3
image_credit: Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Rover on young mare basalt in Mare Imbrium.

name: Chang'e 4
image_credit: CSNA/Siyu Zhang/Kevin M. Gill, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: First landing on the far side, inside Von Karman crater.

name: Chang'e 5
image_credit: China News Service, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Sample return from young basalt in Oceanus Procellarum.

name: Chang'e 6
why_it_matters: First far-side sample return, South Pole-Aitken basin.

name: Marius Hills Pit
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: 40 m deep skylight in a sinuous rille, possible entrance to a lava tube.

name: Mare Tranquillitatis Pit
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Deep pit near Apollo 11 with an overhanging wall. A candidate shelter site.

name: Mare Ingenii Pit
image_credit: James Stuby based on NASA image, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Far-side pit in a swirl region with strong magnetic anomalies.

name: Lacus Mortis Pit
image_credit: NASA / LRO_LROC_TEAM, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Pit with a visible ramp from the rim to the floor.

name: Aristarchus plateau
image_credit: James Stuby based on NASA image, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Volcanic plateau with pyroclastic deposits and a very young crater.

name: Gruithuisen domes
why_it_matters: Unusual silica-rich volcanic domes.

name: Reiner Gamma
image_credit: LRO WAC science team, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Bright swirl on a magnetic anomaly.

name: Schrödinger basin
image_credit: NASA (image by Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Well-preserved basin with pyroclastic deposits and a peak ring.

name: Rima Bode pyroclastics
why_it_matters: Dark mantling deposit with possible oxygen and metal resources.

name: Compton-Belkovich
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Thorium-rich silicic volcanic feature on the far side.

name: Ina
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: D-shaped depression with very young-looking volcanic material.

name: Jezero Crater
image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Ancient lake delta in a crater, explored for signs of past life and collecting samples.

name: Gale Crater
image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/DLR/FU Berlin/MSSS, see Commons, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Crater with a 5 km layered mound, showing a long record of wet and dry conditions.

name: Meridiani Planum
image_credit: Jim Bell and the Opportunity Pancam Team, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Flat plain with hematite and sulfate rock, a classic dry, dusty Mars surface.

name: Gusev Crater
image_credit: NASA/JPL, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Crater with basalt plains and the silica-rich Columbia Hills.

name: Oxia Planum
image_credit: NASA Public domainPublic domainfalsefalse This file is in the public domain in t, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Clay-rich plain chosen for the ExoMars rover to look for traces of life.

name: Elysium Planitia (InSight)
image_credit: ESA/Mars Express/Visual Monitoring Camera, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Smooth flat plain where InSight listened to marsquakes.

name: Utopia Planitia (Viking 2)
image_credit: NASA/JPL, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Northern plain with ice near the surface, landing site of Viking 2.

name: Utopia Planitia (Zhurong)
image_credit: 中国新闻网, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Southern Utopia plain explored by China's Zhurong rover.

name: Chryse Planitia (Viking 1)
image_credit: "Roel van der Hoorn (Van der Hoorn)", Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Large lowland at the end of giant outflow channels.

name: Ares Vallis (Pathfinder)
image_credit: NASA/JPL, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Flood-carved valley with a mix of rocks.

name: Phoenix landing site (Green Valley)
image_credit: NASA/JPL/Corby Waste, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Polar plain where Phoenix dug up water ice a few centimetres down.

name: Arcadia Planitia shallow ice
image_credit: Chmee2, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Plain with ice buried just below the surface, a candidate for water in a first base.

name: Deuteronilus Mensae
image_credit: Jim Secosky modified NASA image. NASA/USGS/Secosky, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Mid-latitude region with glacier-like flows covered by dust and likely rich in ice.

name: Mawrth Vallis
image_credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin, CC BY 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Valley with a thick layered record of clays, a top science target.

name: Eberswalde crater
image_credit: NASA/JPL/Malin Space Science Systems, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Crater holding a well-preserved river delta.

name: Holden crater
image_credit: NASA, modified by Chmee2, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Crater with layered lake deposits and megabreccia.

name: Nili Fossae
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Trough system with carbonate and clay-bearing rocks.

name: Columbia Hills
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Hills inside Gusev with silica deposits that may be from hot springs.

name: Hebrus Valles
image_credit: Jim Secosky modified NASA photo., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Low-lying outflow-channel region near ice and lava, proposed as an exploration zone.

name: Arsia Mons skylights
image_credit: NASA/MOLA Science Team, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Deep pits on the flank of a giant volcano, possible entrances to lava tubes.

name: Noctis Landing
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Canyon-network region with water-related minerals, proposed for a crewed landing.

name: Erebus Montes
image_credit: Jim Secosky modified nasa image., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Mid-latitude mountains with ice-rich flows.

name: Phlegra Montes
image_credit: Martin Pauer (Power), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Mid-latitude hills with glacier-like ice deposits.

name: Melas Chasma
image_credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / Arizona State University, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Deep central canyon of Valles Marineris with layered rock and sulfate minerals.

name: Hellas rim
image_credit: NASA/JPL/USGS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
why_it_matters: Edge of the deepest basin on Mars, where air pressure is highest.
